# Frederick Terman and the Research University {#sec-3-10}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1942–1945
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does wartime research become peacetime monopoly?

**The answer.** Deliberately, by one man who wrote it down in advance. Terman
spent the war running a laboratory of eight hundred people at Harvard, learned
how federal money, secrecy, procurement, and mass technical staffing actually
worked, and came back to Stanford intending to build a permanent peacetime
version. Silicon Valley is not an accident. It is a plan, executed by its
author.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, with the
university as the converter — and the chapter where the book's central
institution acquires its modern function. Terman's insight is that the wartime
funding channel need never close if the university makes itself indispensable to
it.

**The key fact.** Terman directed Harvard's Radio Research Laboratory from 1942,
working on radar countermeasures, and its staff numbered in the hundreds. He
arrived back at Stanford in 1946 having managed a research organisation larger
than Stanford's entire pre-war engineering school.

**The human anchor.** Terman on a train back to California in 1945, with a
management playbook and a grievance: his university had been a bystander to the
biggest scientific mobilisation in history, and he did not intend for that to
happen again.

**Excluded voices.** The classified nature of most of it, which means the public
paid for research it could not examine — a structural exclusion that Act III ch.
7 will turn into a campus revolt.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that Silicon Valley's institutional architecture
was designed rather than emergent by showing its designer state the plan before
executing it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Frederick Terman spent the war running Harvard's Radio Research Laboratory, an
organisation of several hundred people working on radar countermeasures with a
budget larger than Stanford's entire pre-war engineering programme. He returned
to Palo Alto in 1946 to a department of a few dozen, carrying a management
playbook and a grievance.

The grievance matters. Stanford had been a bystander to the largest scientific
mobilisation in history while MIT and Harvard captured the contracts, and
Terman's diagnosis of why is the origin of everything in Act II. Silicon Valley
is not an accident or an emergence. It is a plan, written down in advance,
executed by its author over three decades.

What the war taught him was operational: how federal money actually moved, how
procurement and classification worked, how to staff a technical organisation at
speed, and — most importantly — that the government would fund science
indefinitely if the science was necessary. Vannevar Bush's *Science, the Endless
Frontier* made the intellectual case for permanence in 1945, and the funding
channel it proposed was going to exist whether or not Stanford was on it.

Terman's answer was concentration. Rather than becoming adequate across many
fields, Stanford would build what he called steeples of excellence — a small
number of areas where federal money was flowing, in which the university would
make itself indispensable. Electronics and microwaves first. Follow the money
and then become the bottleneck it must pass through.

The chapter also plants the asset that Act III will pay off, and does not explain
it yet: eight thousand acres of land that the Founding Grant forbids the
university to sell.

The public paid for most of the research and, because much of it was classified,
could not examine it. The chapter names that as a structural exclusion, and
points forward to the campus revolt it eventually produces.

A designer, a plan, a permanent funding channel, and an enormous piece of
unsellable land. Everything Act III needs is now in place.
:::

1. **Hook.** Terman in 1945, having run eight hundred people, returning to a
   department of a few dozen. The ambition is a response to a slight.
2. **The Radio Research Laboratory.** Radar countermeasures, the scale, the
   money, and what running it taught him: budgets, secrecy, procurement,
   staffing at speed.
3. **What the war proved.** That government would fund science indefinitely if
   the science was necessary. The channel exists; the question is who it flows
   through.
4. **Vannevar Bush and the OSRD.** The architecture of wartime research funding,
   and *Science, the Endless Frontier* in 1945. The intellectual case for
   permanence.
5. **Where Stanford stood.** Behind. MIT and Harvard captured the contracts.
   Terman's diagnosis of why.
6. **The plan.** Steeples of excellence: concentrate resources on a few fields
   where federal money is going, and become indispensable in those rather than
   adequate everywhere.
7. **The land.** Note it and hold it — eight thousand acres that cannot be sold
   under the Founding Grant, and therefore must be leased. Act III ch. 1 pays

8. **The excluded.** Classification. Public money, unexaminable results.
9. **Landing.** A designer, a plan, a funding channel, and an enormous piece of
   unsellable land. Everything Act III needs is now in place.

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does wartime research become peacetime monopoly?
:::

Frederick Terman spent the Second World War in Cambridge, Massachusetts, running
a laboratory of some eight hundred people with a budget larger than the whole of
Stanford's pre-war engineering programme.

The Radio Research Laboratory, established at Harvard in 1942, worked on radar
countermeasures — jamming, deception, and the detection of enemy radar. It was a
serious operation with a serious product; Allied bombing operations depended on
its output, and the aluminium chaff dropped to blind German radar came out of
this work.

Terman came back to Palo Alto in 1946 to a department of a few dozen people,
carrying a management playbook and a grievance.

## The grievance

The grievance matters more than the playbook, because it explains the intensity
of what followed.

Stanford had been a bystander to the largest scientific mobilisation in history.
The contracts had gone to MIT, to Harvard, to Caltech, and to Bell Laboratories.
Berkeley, thirty miles away, had built cyclotrons and staffed the Manhattan
Project. Stanford had contributed individuals — Terman among them — to other
people's laboratories.

Terman's diagnosis was not that Stanford had been unlucky. It was that Stanford
had been the wrong shape. Federal science money went to institutions that were
already visibly excellent in the fields the government needed, and it went to
people the men making the decisions already knew. Stanford was adequate across
many fields and pre-eminent in none, which meant that when a decision-maker in
Washington needed a laboratory, Stanford was on nobody's list.

He wrote it down and he said it repeatedly for the next twenty years.

## What the war actually taught

The operational education was the more valuable part, and it consisted of things
that cannot be learned from outside.

He learned how federal research money actually moved: who decided, on what
timetable, against what criteria, and what a proposal had to look like. He
learned procurement and classification, and how to run an organisation in which
most of the staff cannot discuss most of the work. He learned how to recruit and
manage several hundred technical people at speed, which almost nobody in
American academic life had ever done.

And he learned the thing that made the rest of it worth knowing: that the
funding would not stop. Total war had established that scientific capability was
a strategic asset, and no government that had learned that lesson was going to
unlearn it.

Vannevar Bush made the intellectual case in *Science, the Endless Frontier*,
delivered to the president in July 1945. Bush argued that basic research was the
source of practical advance, that it would be underfunded by private industry
because its returns were unappropriable, and that the federal government should
therefore fund it permanently — through universities, with the scientists
themselves controlling the allocation.

That report is the founding document of the postwar American research system,
and Terman read it as a business plan.

## Steeples of excellence

His strategy had a name, and it was the opposite of what most universities were
attempting.

The conventional postwar ambition was breadth: build up every department, become
comprehensive, cover the field. Terman argued for concentration. Identify a
small number of areas where federal money was going and where Stanford could
plausibly become pre-eminent, and put everything into those. He called them
steeples of excellence — narrow, tall, and visible from a distance.

He chose electronics and microwave physics, which is where the defence money was
going, and he recruited accordingly: senior people poached from other
institutions with the promise of resources, and money to build around them.

The method had two features that made it work and that generalise. It followed
the funding rather than the discipline, which meant the university's research
agenda was substantially set by federal priorities. And it was ruthless about
what it declined to support, which is why it succeeded where more equitable
strategies did not.

Stanford's engineering and physics departments moved into the front rank within
about fifteen years. The Microwave Laboratory and then the linear accelerator
followed. By the 1960s Stanford was one of the largest recipients of federal
research funding in the country, having received essentially none of the wartime
contracts twenty years earlier.

## The asset nobody had used

There is one more piece, and Terman appears not to have recognised its full
value immediately.

The university owned eight thousand acres of the San Francisco Peninsula, and
under the Founding Grant of 1885 it could not sell any of it. For sixty years
this had been treated as a constraint. The land was leased for grazing, used for
agriculture, and otherwise sat there, an enormous illiquid asset generating
almost nothing.

An asset that cannot be sold can be leased. And a university that leases land to
companies whose staff it trains, whose research it partners on, and whose
legitimacy it underwrites is not a landlord in any ordinary sense.

Act III opens on the day someone acts on this.

## Recruiting

The method deserves a section, because it is the mechanism by which a regional
university became a national one and because it is not what universities
normally do.

Terman recruited the way a company acquires a business. He identified
individuals whose presence would attract federal funding and other researchers,
and he offered them resources rather than salary — laboratory space, equipment
budgets, graduate students, and the freedom to build a group. He then used their
arrival to recruit the next tier, on the argument that the field was moving to
Palo Alto.

The clearest single instance is the Varian brothers, Russell and Sigurd, who
with William Hansen had developed the klystron tube at Stanford before the war
under an arrangement that gave the university a share of the royalties. The
klystron mattered enormously to radar and later to microwave communications and
to accelerators. Varian Associates was founded in 1948, and in 1951 it became
the first tenant of the industrial park.

That sequence is the whole model in one company: university research, a
licensing arrangement that pays the university, a spin-out firm founded by the
researchers, and a lease on university land. Every element of Act III is present
in 1951, in a single tenancy agreement.

Terman also encouraged faculty to consult for industry and to found companies,
at a time when most universities regarded both as distractions or conflicts. He
regarded them as the point. A professor with a company brings in contracts,
places graduates, and generates the reputation that attracts the next recruit.

## The classified problem

The chapter has to name the cost, and here it is structural rather than
personal.

A substantial and growing fraction of the research Terman built was classified.
The public funded it, the university performed it, and the public could not
examine the results. There was no mechanism by which a citizen, a journalist, or
a legislator could evaluate what was being done with the money, and the people
best placed to evaluate it were the people receiving it.

Terman regarded this as unproblematic and most of his contemporaries agreed. It
was wartime practice continued into a cold war that appeared to be permanent,
and the alternative — a research establishment that discussed its work in public
— was not on offer while the Soviet Union existed.

It became a problem in 1969, when a few hundred students walked into a building
and shut it down. Act III chapter 7 is that chapter, and the target they chose
was the laboratory Terman built.

## The plan and its author

Silicon Valley is not an emergence and it is not an accident. It is a plan,
written down in advance by a dean of engineering who had spent three years
watching the federal government spend money on other people's universities and
had worked out precisely why.

He had the diagnosis by 1945, the strategy by the late 1940s, the land by
inheritance, and the funding channel by act of Congress. What he needed next was
tenants.
